## One-Sample t-tests

A **one-sample t-test** is used to make inference about a population mean using a single sample.

**Conditions:**

- Random sample from the population
- $n > 30$, __or__ the original variable follows a normal distribution in the population

$$H_0: \mu = \mu_0 \qquad \text{vs.} \qquad H_A: \mu \ne \mu_0 \ \ (\text{or} \ <, \ >)$$

where $\mu$ is the population mean.

**Motivating example:** A clinical trial is testing a new antihypertensive drug ("Drug A") against a placebo in patients with Stage 1 hypertension. Each of the __200 patients__ (100 per group) has a __baseline__ systolic blood pressure (SBP, in mmHg) and a __12-week follow-up__ SBP. We'll use this same trial throughout Module 3 to practice different tests. The data are stored in `htn_trial`, with columns `group`, `sbp_baseline`, `sbp_followup`, and `sbp_change` (follow-up minus baseline).

For this first test, we'll focus on a simple question: __is the average follow-up SBP in the Drug A group below the clinical hypertension threshold of 130 mmHg?__

### Creating a Factor Variable

Right now, the treatment group is stored in `htn_trial$group_num` as a __number__ (1 = Drug A, 2 = Placebo). If we tried to use this numeric column directly in later analyses (like ANOVA, in Module 4), R would incorrectly treat it as a continuous predictor instead of a grouping variable! Let's fix that now by creating a proper factor column called `group`.

```{code-blanks-instructions}
Fill in the code below to create a new column, `group`, that labels `group_num == 1` as `"Drug A"` and `group_num == 2` as `"Placebo"`.
```

```{code-blanks}
#| blank:
#|   target: group_num
#|   prefill: false
#|   occurrence: 1
#|   match: token
#| blank:
#|   target: "Drug A"
#|   prefill: false
#|   occurrence: 1
#|   match: token
#| blank:
#|   target: "Placebo"
#|   prefill: false
#|   occurrence: 1
#|   match: token

# create a labeled factor variable for treatment group
htn_trial = htn_trial %>%
  mutate(group = factor(group_num, levels = c(1, 2), labels = c("Drug A", "Placebo")))

# check that it worked
head(htn_trial)
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

``` r
# create a labeled factor variable for treatment group
htn_trial = htn_trial %>%
  mutate(group = factor(group_num, levels = c(1, 2), labels = c("Drug A", "Placebo")))

# check that it worked
head(htn_trial)
```

You should now see a new column, `group`, with labels `"Drug A"` and `"Placebo"` instead of `1` and `2`. We'll use this labeled version throughout the rest of this document (and throughout Module 3).
:::

### Checking Conditions

```{code-blanks-instructions}
Filter `htn_trial` to only the Drug A group (recall `group_num == 1` is Drug A), and plot a histogram of `sbp_followup` to check the shape of the distribution.
```

```{code-blanks}
#| blank:
#|   target: group_num
#|   prefill: false
#|   occurrence: 1

#| blank:
#|   target: sbp_followup
#|   prefill: false

# filter to the Drug A group and plot a histogram of follow-up SBP
htn_trial %>%
  filter(group_num == 1) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = sbp_followup)) +
  geom_histogram(fill = "blue", bins = 20) +
  theme_bw()
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

``` r
# filter to the Drug A group and plot a histogram of follow-up SBP
htn_trial %>%
  filter(group_num == 1) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = sbp_followup)) +
  geom_histogram(fill = "blue", bins = 20) +
  theme_bw()
```

You should see a roughly __bell-shaped, symmetric__ distribution centered somewhere in the 120s. Either way, with __n = 100__, we'd be comfortable relying on the CLT even if the data were somewhat non-normal.
:::

### Calculating the Test Statistic

Suppose a summary of the Drug A group's follow-up SBP showed a sample mean of $\bar{x} = 128$ and sample standard deviation of $s = 9$, based on $n = 100$ patients. We want to test $H_0: \mu = 130$ vs. $H_A: \mu < 130$.

Recall the formula for a one-sample t-test statistic:

$$t_{obs} = \dfrac{\bar{x} - \mu_0}{s / \sqrt{n}}$$

```{code-blanks-instructions}
Fill in the code below to calculate the standard error and the test statistic, testing against $\mu_0 = 130$.
```

```{code-blanks}
#| blank:
#|   target: s
#|   prefill: false
#|   occurrence: 3
#|   match: token
#| blank:
#|   target: n
#|   prefill: false
#|   occurrence: 3
#|   match: token
#| blank:
#|   target: xbar
#|   prefill: false
#|   occurrence: 3
#|   match: token
#| blank:
#|   target: mu0
#|   prefill: false
#|   occurrence: 2
#|   match: token
#| blank:
#|   target: se
#|   prefill: false
#|   occurrence: 2
#|   match: token

# summary statistics
xbar = mean(htn_trial$sbp_followup[htn_trial$group_num==1])
mu0 = 130
s = sd(htn_trial$sbp_followup[htn_trial$group_num==1])
n = sum(htn_trial$group_num==1)

# print values
xbar ;  s; n

# standard error
se = s / sqrt(n)

# test statistic
t_obs = (xbar - mu0) / se
t_obs
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

``` r
# summary statistics
xbar = mean(htn_trial$sbp_followup[htn_trial$group_num==1])
mu0 = 130
s = sd(htn_trial$sbp_followup[htn_trial$group_num==1])
n = sum(htn_trial$group_num==1)

# print values
xbar ; s; n

# standard error
se = s / sqrt(n)

# test statistic
t_obs = (xbar - mu0) / se
t_obs
```
[[1] 127.3865
[1] 130
[1] 8.059693
[1] 100
[1] -3.24262{style="font-family: 'Monaco'; font-weight: 500; font-size : 12px;"}

Our observed test statistic is negative, consistent with a sample mean (127.4) that's below the hypothesized value (130).
:::

### Rejection Region

Since $H_A: \mu < \mu_0$, this is a __one-sided, lower-tailed__ test. The rejection region is in the __left tail__ of the $t$ distribution with $n - 1$ degrees of freedom.

```{code-blanks-instructions}
Find the critical value (rejection region cutoff) for a lower-tailed test with $\alpha = 0.05$ and $n - 1 = 99$ degrees of freedom.
```

```{code-blanks}
#| blank:
#|   target: 0.05
#|   prefill: false
#|   occurrence: 1
#|   match: token
#| blank:
#|   target: n - 1
#|   prefill: false
#|   occurrence: 1
#|   match: token

# significance level
alph = 0.05

# lower-tailed rejection region cutoff
qt(alph, df = n - 1)
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

``` r
# significance level
alph = 0.05

# lower-tailed rejection region cutoff
qt(alph, df = n - 1)
```
[[1] -1.660391]{style="font-family: 'Monaco'; font-weight: 500; font-size : 12px;"}

Since our observed test statistic (-3.24) is __more negative__ than this cutoff (-1.66), it falls in the rejection region.
:::

```{code-blanks-response}
Based on the rejection region above, would we reject or fail to reject $H_0$? What would that mean in the context of this study?
```

### P-value

```{code-blanks-instructions}
Calculate the one-sided (lower-tailed) p-value corresponding to our test statistic, using `pt()`. Since we want the area to the **left** of our test statistic, we can use the default `lower.tail = TRUE` (the default, so you don't need to specify it).
```

```{code-blanks}
#| blank:
#|   target: n - 1
#|   prefill: false
#|   occurrence: 1
#|   match: token

# one-sided (lower-tailed) p-value
pt(t_obs, df = n - 1)
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

``` r
# one-sided (lower-tailed) p-value
pt(t_obs, df = n - 1)
```
[[1] 0.0008073392]{style="font-family: 'Monaco'; font-weight: 500; font-size : 12px;"}

This p-value (0.0008) is __less than 0.05__, so we would reject $H_0$ and conclude that average follow-up SBP in the Drug A group is below 130&mdash;consistent with our rejection region result above.
:::

### Confidence Interval

A one-sided 95% confidence interval for $H_A: \mu < \mu_0$ has the form $\left(-\infty, \ \bar{x} + t^* \cdot se\right)$, where $t^*$ is the __upper__ 95th-percentile critical value (note: this is a different cutoff than the one we used for the rejection region above, since that one captured the lower 5% rather than the upper 5%).

```{code-blanks-instructions}
Calculate the upper bound of a one-sided 95% confidence interval for the population mean follow-up SBP.
```

```{code-blanks}
#| blank:
#|   target: 0.95
#|   prefill: false
#|   occurrence: 1
#|   match: token
#| blank:
#|   target: n - 1
#|   prefill: false
#|   occurrence: 1
#|   match: token

# one-sided 95% CI upper bound
xbar + qt(0.95, df = n - 1) * se
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

``` r
# one-sided 95% CI upper bound
xbar + qt(0.95, df = n - 1) * se
```
[[1] 128.7248]{style="font-family: 'Monaco'; font-weight: 500; font-size : 12px;"}

We are 95% confident that the true average follow-up SBP in the Drug A group is __no more than about 128.7__&mdash;which is indeed below our threshold of 130. This agrees with our rejection region and p-value results, as it should, since all three methods lead to the same conclusion.
:::

### Using `t.test()`

All of this can be done in a single step using the built-in `t.test()` function.

```{code-blanks-instructions}
Fill in the code below to run a one-sample t-test on the Drug A group's `sbp_followup`, testing against $\mu_0 = 130$ with the alternative hypothesis that the mean is __less than__ 130.
```

```{code-blanks}
#| blank:
#|   target: group_num
#|   prefill: false
#|   occurrence: 1
#|   match: token
#| blank:
#|   target: 130
#|   prefill: false
#|   occurrence: 1
#|   match: token
#| blank:
#|   target: "less"
#|   prefill: false
#|   occurrence: 1
#|   match: token

# one-sample t-test
drug_a_followup = htn_trial %>% filter(group_num == 1) %>% pull(sbp_followup)
t.test(drug_a_followup, mu = 130, alternative = "less")
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

``` r
# one-sample t-test
drug_a_followup = htn_trial %>% filter(group_num == 1) %>% pull(sbp_followup)
t.test(drug_a_followup, mu = 130, alternative = "less")
```

We can see that the numbers here match out by-hand calculations.
:::

```{code-blanks-response}
Compare the output of `t.test()` to our manual calculations above. Are the general conclusions (reject vs. fail to reject) consistent?
```

### One-Sided vs. Two-Sided Tests

```{code-blanks-instructions}
Modify the code above to run the __same test__, but using a two-sided alternative instead.
```

```{code-blanks}
#| blank:
#|   target: 130
#|   prefill: false
#|   occurrence: 1
#|   match: token
#| blank:
#|   target: "two.sided"
#|   prefill: false
#|   occurrence: 1
#|   match: token

# two-sided one-sample t-test
t.test(drug_a_followup, mu = 130, alternative = "two.sided")
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

``` r
# two-sided one-sample t-test
t.test(drug_a_followup, mu = 130, alternative = "two.sided")
```

The test statistic stays the same, but the __p-value doubles__ compared to the one-sided test, and the confidence interval becomes __two-sided__ (both a lower and upper bound) instead of having an infinite lower bound.
:::

```{code-blanks-response}
In general, when is it appropriate to use a one-sided test instead of a two-sided test? Why is it considered poor practice to choose the direction of a one-sided test *after* looking at your data?
```

## Sample Size and Power

Before collecting data, we often want to know how large a sample we'll need to detect a meaningful effect, or how much power a given sample size will provide. R's `power.t.test()` function handles this for one-sample (and paired) t-tests.

```{code-blanks-instructions}
Suppose we want to detect a true difference (`delta`) of __2 mmHg__ from the null value, assuming a standard deviation of __9__, with a significance level of __0.05__ and __80% power__, using a __one-sided__ test. Fill in the code below to find the required sample size.
```

```{code-blanks}
#| blank:
#|   target: 2
#|   prefill: false
#|   occurrence: 1
#|   match: token
#| blank:
#|   target: 9
#|   prefill: false
#|   occurrence: 1
#|   match: token
#| blank:
#|   target: 0.05
#|   prefill: false
#|   occurrence: 1
#|   match: token
#| blank:
#|   target: 0.8
#|   prefill: false
#|   occurrence: 1
#|   match: token
#| blank:
#|   target: "one.sample"
#|   prefill: false
#|   occurrence: 1
#|   match: token
#| blank:
#|   target: "one.sided"
#|   prefill: false
#|   occurrence: 1
#|   match: token

# required sample size for 80% power
power.t.test(delta = 2, 
             sd = 9, 
             sig.level = 0.05,
             power = 0.8, 
             type = "one.sample", 
             alternative = "one.sided")
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

``` r
# required sample size for 80% power
power.t.test(delta = 2, 
             sd = 9, 
             sig.level = 0.05,
             power = 0.8, 
             type = "one.sample", 
             alternative = "one.sided")
```

[n = 126.5606]{style="font-family: 'Monaco'; font-weight: 500; font-size : 12px;"}

We would need about __127 participants__ (always round up!) to have an 80% chance of detecting a true difference of 2 mmHg, if one exists.
:::

```{code-blanks-instructions}
Now suppose we only have __100 participants__ available (as in our actual Drug A group). Fill in the code below to calculate the power of our test under the same assumptions (`delta = 2`, `sd = 9`, one-sample, one-sided).
```

```{code-blanks}
#| blank:
#|   target: 100
#|   prefill: false
#|   occurrence: 2
#|   match: token
#| blank:
#|   target: 2
#|   prefill: false
#|   occurrence: 1
#|   match: token
#| blank:
#|   target: 9
#|   prefill: false
#|   occurrence: 1
#|   match: token
#| blank:
#|   target: "one.sample"
#|   prefill: false
#|   occurrence: 1
#|   match: token
#| blank:
#|   target: "one.sided"
#|   prefill: false
#|   occurrence: 1
#|   match: token

# power with n = 100
power.t.test(n = 100, 
             delta = 2, 
             sd = 9,
             type = "one.sample", 
             alternative = "one.sided")
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

``` r
# power with n = 100
power.t.test(n = 100, 
             delta = 2, 
             sd = 9,
             type = "one.sample", 
             alternative = "one.sided")
```

[power = 0.71299]{style="font-family: 'Monaco'; font-weight: 500; font-size : 12px;"}

With 100 participants, our power is about __71.3%__&mdash;a bit short of the 80% we were aiming for.
:::
